newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan dealers worry despite recent stock gains.
newsitem.headline: Japan dealers worry despite recent stock gains.

text.p: Buying by pension funds has helped lift the Tokyo stock market out of its doldrums, but brokerages are starting to worry that the recent rise in stocks may not have been very profitable for them.
In order to meet the flood of orders from funds, dealers have been using margin trades to come up with the desired shares and have built up a hefty amount of short positions in the process.
Brokerage sources fear that the dealers may have to start covering their shorts soon and bear hefty losses arising from the paying of borrowing fees.
In the past few sessions, the number of shares with those fees has exceeded 200.
"Dealers' own positions have tripled from normal levels due to buy orders from pension funds," a broker at a second-tier brokerage said on Friday.

"The margin-trade shorts are being hedged using TOPIX futures but the momentum of the market is not showing signs of abating and the order volumes are quite hefty so the positions are becoming difficult to cover."
At some brokerages, dealers' shorts are coming close to, or exceeding, the maximum amount allowed.
"The risks may be growing to a level which cannot be covered by commissions alone," said a broker at a second-tier brokerage.

But despite the lofty mood of the market and fears of losses stemming from the rise, market participants are beginning to speculate on when the fund allocations will run dry and what will happen afterwards.
In the course of about two weeks, the Nikkei average has gained about 1,000 points, thanks mainly to pension fund buying.
Most believe that after Japan's "Golden Week" holidays next week the funds will run out and the market will fall back into the rut it was in.
"Foreign investors' moves and that of currencies are unclear, so no one can guess who will buy after the pension funds stop," a source at a foreign brokerage said.
"Once the fresh money stops, there may be an over-supply, and the market could be forced to correct itself and wait for fresh allocations," a "Big Four" broker added.
